# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
I've read it. Here's my restatement, then my assessment.

## What the paper reports

- **Design.** 61 self-selected organisations (from 70 enrolled; 9 withdrew during preparation) cut scheduled hours from 40 to 32 at full pay for six months, after two months of preparation. There was no control group, and each organisation is compared with its own prior six months.
- **Primary outcome.** A monthly output index completed by each organisation's pilot manager (100 = unchanged), based on whatever records they held. It ended at 98.7. Dividing by 0.8 gives "+23.4% output per scheduled hour".
- **Secondary outcomes.**
  - Revenue +1.4% year on year (52 of 61 organisations reporting).
  - Sick days −36%, resignations −56%, frequent burnout down from 38% to 21%.
  - Energy up 0.61 SD at month three and 0.29 SD at month six.
- **Continuation.** 56 of 61 organisations continued.
- **Conclusions.** The model is "sector-general", fatigue reduction is the most plausible mechanism, and the limitations are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors."

I checked the arithmetic. The per-hour figures follow from the index values, and the employee-weighted mean of 98.7 and the organisation and employee totals reconcile. The numbers are internally consistent. The problems are in what they're taken to show.

## What the data support, at full weight

Across 61 organisations, managers reported output close to baseline after a 20% cut in scheduled hours. Absence, resignations and burnout fell substantially. Most organisations chose to continue. That is a notable result, and it shouldn't be hedged into "promising". It establishes that, for organisations that volunteer and prepare, a 32-hour schedule was workable for six months without managers reporting a large output loss.

## Where the conclusions outrun the evidence

**1. The "sector-general" conclusion is contradicted by the paper's own data.** This is the most important problem. Combining the continuation section with Table 1:

| | Organisations | Reverted | Reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 3 | 50% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 2 | 40% |
| All other sectors | 50 | 0 | 0% |

The two sectors with the lowest output indices are the only sectors where any organisation reverted, and they did so at high rates. Retail also had the largest output fall (−6.9%). The paper reports "92% continued" and "gains in every sector" separately, and so never sets these figures side by side. Read together, the evidence points to sector *heterogeneity*, which is the opposite of the stated conclusion.

Six retail organisations, self-selected, can't establish sector-generality in any case. The defensible statement is: "Output was maintained in knowledge-work sectors. In retail and hospitality and in healthcare administration, output fell more and many organisations reverted. Whether the model works in coverage-dependent sectors is open."

**2. The "gain in every sector" is close to built into the method.** Output per scheduled hour is the index divided by 0.8. Any organisation reporting output above 80 shows a per-hour gain. So "every sector shows a substantial increase" mostly restates "no sector reported output below 80". The 23.4% figure is a transformation of the 98.7, not independent evidence. The Limitations section then cites the result's "size and consistency" as a reason to discount the limitations. That is circular, because both properties come from the division.

**3. The primary outcome is the weakest measurement in the study.** The index is a judgment by the manager responsible for the pilot's success, on a scale anchored at "100 = unchanged", using records that vary by organisation. That design invites values near 100 regardless of what happened. Limitation 3 acknowledges this but doesn't follow it through: the headline rests entirely on this measure. Where objective records exist (billable hours, tickets closed, units sold, cases processed), even a subsample of organisations reporting them alongside their index would show how far the two agree.

**4. "Per scheduled hour" is not "per hour worked".** Limitation 4 says actual hours weren't collected. If people worked on their day off or lengthened other days, the true per-hour gain is smaller, possibly much smaller. The issue is sharpest in retail and hospitality: 17 organisations staggered days off "to maintain coverage", and if opening hours were unchanged, total staff hours may not have fallen much at all. This limitation bears directly on the headline number, not just its precision.

**5. Revenue is presented as reassurance it doesn't provide.**
- The +1.4% is presumably nominal. If the pilot ran in 2023, inflation in most economies was well above 1.4%, so real revenue may have *fallen*. The paper should state the deflator, or report the figure as nominal and say what it implies.
- Nine organisations didn't report revenue, so the paper should say which ones, and whether they include the reverters.

**6. The secondary outcomes have uncontrolled confounds the paper doesn't mention.**
- *Seasonality.* Revenue was compared year on year to remove seasonality, but sick days and resignations were compared with the six months before the pilot. If those months included winter, part of the −36% in sick days is seasonal. The same seasonal comparison should be applied to sick days and resignations.
- *Labour market.* Quit rates fell in many economies through 2023, and with no control group, part of the −56% may reflect that.
- *Changed incentives.* A four-day week at full pay is a 25% rise in hourly pay. Lower resignations is the expected response to a large benefit and says little about productivity.

**7. The fatigue mechanism is stated more strongly than its evidence.** Nothing in the study separates fatigue from the process changes managers described: fewer meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58 managers), focus blocks, cut reporting. The energy data, rising 0.61 SD then falling to 0.29 SD, are at least as consistent with novelty fading as with sustained rest.

This matters for policy. If the gains come mainly from process changes, organisations could get much of the benefit without cutting hours. Both explanations should be reported as candidates, along with what would distinguish them (for example, a comparison arm that makes the process changes at 40 hours).

**8. Continuation is weaker evidence than presented.**
- Reverting means taking back a benefit staff now hold, which is costly regardless of how productive the arrangement was.
- The rate is 56 of 61 only after excluding the 9 enrolled organisations that withdrew "chiefly for scheduling reasons". Measured against enrolment it is 56 of 70 (80%). Those withdrawals are themselves informative about where scheduling is hard, so it would help to report their sectors.

**Smaller points:**
- "64% rated own productivity higher than before" needs the rest of the distribution: how many said lower?
- Employee weighting is reasonable, but given the sector heterogeneity, an unweighted organisation-level summary would be a useful check.

## How I'd rewrite the conclusion

> In 61 self-selected organisations, a 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay was accompanied by manager-reported output close to baseline and by large reductions in sickness absence, resignations and burnout. Results differed by sector. In professional services, software, marketing and non-profits, output was maintained and no organisation reverted. In retail and hospitality and in healthcare administration, output fell further and 5 of 11 organisations reverted.
>
> Because output was manager-assessed, actual hours were not measured and there was no comparison group, the size of any gain in output per hour is uncertain. Whether it comes from reduced fatigue or from the process changes organisations made is open. Further pilots should include a comparison group, objective output measures and recorded hours.

This keeps every finding the data support at full strength. It reports sector heterogeneity as found rather than calling the model sector-general, and it marks the mechanism and the magnitude as open, along with what would close them.
